items.title: The AI boom hits its ‘final stages’ as Anthropic goes public and the jobless-growth economy delivers neither jobs nor growth
items.summary:
The AI stock boom is “in its final stages,” Capital Economics wrote on Monday, and what does the U.S. economy really have to show for it? 

Anthropic is going public, anyway, on Thursday, in a deal estimated to raise about $64.35 billion at the top of its range. That’s nearly twice what every U.S. IPO raised together last quarter, per Renaissance Capital .

If Capital Economics is right, the timing is bad for more than Anthropic’s bankers. The AI boom has been carrying the growth half of what Goldman Sachs economists called “jobless growth.” The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter while employers added an average of 48,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September—before a massive 165,000 gain in October. AI spending drove more than half of business-investment growth in the first three quarters of the year, Goldman estimates.

Take the boom away and you could be left with the jobless part. J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s David Kelly already sees real GDP growth slowing to 1.6% over the next four quarters, with hiring stuck near 50,000 a month.

Capital Economics markets economist Joe Maher pointed to falling share issuance and “investors’ waning appetite for new shares of AI-firms at lofty valuations.” Anthropic, he wrote, is “a key test.” 

By Kelly’s math, two years of 2.3% growth “should have led to a monthly gain of roughly 155,000 net new jobs.” Instead, the economy got just 48,000. Kelly mainly blames “a lack of available workers due to a sharp reversal of immigration policy.”

The bar has dropped to match. Morgan Stanley’s research digest…
items.t: The AI boom hits its ‘final stages’ as Anthropic goes public and the jobless-growth economy delivers neither jobs nor growth

items.title: Delta CEO Ed Bastian believes ‘human error’ and faulty equipment led to FAA ground stop
items.summary:
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as currently lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.”

Bastian, speaking with Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11.

What led to the FAA ground stop 

Bastian said he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”

Bastian said the router work wasn’t new. “I think they’ve replaced, I understand, close to 70% of the routers already,” he said. L3Harris says the switch to fiber is more than 70% done. “So I…
items.t: Delta CEO Ed Bastian believes ‘human error’ and faulty equipment led to FAA ground stop

items.title: America’s housing squeeze is moving into the middle class
items.summary:
In October 2010, a Vietnam veteran in black gloves and a famous set of whiskers stole a New York governor’s debate at Hofstra University. Jimmy McMillan had founded the Rent Is Too Damn High Party, and the platform spoke for itself.

Sixteen years later, the rent is still too high for nearly half of America’s middle-income renters. Among renters earning $45,000 to $74,999, 49% spent more than 30% of their income on housing in 2024, up 9.5 percentage points since 2019, according to Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies . The share continued to rise most rapidly among middle-income households, research analyst Peyton Whitney wrote in February.

The bottom had nowhere left to go. Some 83% of renters earning under $30,000 were already cost-burdened, a share that “didn’t have much room to grow,” Harvard wrote.

The middle’s way out is narrowing, too. In 2019, roughly half of home listings were affordable to a household earning about $75,000, Harvard managing director Chris Herbert said in June. Now it’s less than a quarter. The center estimates a household needs roughly $120,000 to afford a typical home.

New Bank of America payments data shows the two ends of the ladder spending even greater percentages of their income. About one in four lower-income renters and one in four higher-income mortgage holders now spend more than half their income on housing, according to BofA data through September. The bank’s Nov. 11 note didn’t give a figure for the middle third. 

“Put simply, housing is still taking a big bite out of household budgets across the income spectrum,” the Bank…
items.t: America’s housing squeeze is moving into the middle class

items.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth.
items.summary:
Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon .

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities…
items.t: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth.

items.title: The AI layoff wave never arrived in 2026. Goldman says it’s just delayed
items.summary:
Americans are filing for unemployment at the slowest four-week pace on record. Goldman Sachs gives that about a year.

“This year began with fears of a looming AI-driven layoff wave, but the layoff rate instead remained historically low,” Goldman economists wrote in their 2027 U.S. outlook, published Sunday night. They expect this “slightly softer low-hire, low-fire form of full employment” will last one more year “before AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”

Goldman has been arguing that AI job losses are just waiting on a downturn to be felt in force. In October 2025, Goldman’s U.S. economists David Mericle and Pierfrancesco Mei called “jobless growth” the likely new normal. “History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits,” they predicted.

Last month, Goldman economist Joseph Briggs estimated that up to 9% of workers could be “displaced during the AI transition,” roughly one in 11. He found that “automation-related labor disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns.” The share of Americans in routine jobs, such as clerks, secretaries and machine operators, dropped in steps during the recessions of the early 1980s, 2001, 2008 and 2020, and didn’t climb back. The McKinsey Global Institute has projected that 6 million to 16 million U.S. workers may need to switch occupations by 2035, or about 7% of current employees at the midpoint of that range.

For workers, the effects so far have shown up in stagnant…
items.t: The AI layoff wave never arrived in 2026. Goldman says it’s just delayed

items.title: Existing home sales just hit their lowest level since 2010
items.summary:
Previously owned homes sold at their slowest pace since 2010 in October. Existing home sales fell 5.5% from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, according to the National Association of Realtors . That’s down 8.8% from a year earlier and below the 3.85 million economists expected, according to Goldman Sachs’ tally of forecasts.

The last time sales were this slow, the market was choking on foreclosures. Foreclosures and short sales made up 26% of home sales in 2010, according to RealtyTrac . In October, distressed sales were 2%, NAR said. 

But this time around, nobody is being forced out. The people who own the houses are staying in them, and a big share of them are older. Empty-nest baby boomers own 28% of U.S. homes with three or more bedrooms, while millennials with children own 16%, Redfin found in 2024 Census data. People who did sell in the year through June had owned their homes for a median 12 years, the longest NAR has ever recorded .

Mortgage rates are keeping homeowners locked in, what the industry literally calls “the lock-in effect.” The 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September and 6.25% a year earlier. Nearly half of outstanding mortgages, 49.1%, carry a rate below 4%, Realtor.com found in FHFA data for the second quarter. For many older owners, the rate isn’t even the issue: 57.8% of boomer homeowners have no mortgage at all, according to Redfin.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000,” said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun, who noted the…
items.t: Existing home sales just hit their lowest level since 2010

items.title: Warren Buffett is giving $5.4 billion to his family foundations for Thanksgiving. His advice to everyone else: ‘Be a benefactor for someone else’
items.summary:
Warren Buffett kept his Thanksgiving message short this year, but the amount he gave was anything but small. 

The 96-year-old Berkshire Hathaway chairman emeritus is converting 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and donating them to four of his family’s foundations, according to a Berkshire release published Monday. At the latest Class B price, the donation is worth an eye-popping $5.4 billion. 

The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation (named in honor of Warren’s first wife) will receive shares worth about $2.2 billion. The Sherwood Foundation (led by Warren’s daughter, Susan), the Howard G. Buffett Foundation (run by Warren’s son), and the NoVo Foundation (run by Warren’s other son, Peter) will each get shares worth a little more than $1 billion. 

“Today’s gift is consistent with the plan I have previously described,” Warren Buffett wrote in his annual Thanksgiving letter. “All my Berkshire shares will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal of growing the grants each year.”

He said whether he reaches that goal will largely depend on how the stock market performs between now and his target date. He also said he has full confidence in his three children: “I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity.”

After this gift, Buffett will still own 182,140 Class A shares and 1,162 Class B shares, according to the release. That’s still worth more than $160 billion, assuming the most recent price. 

Buffett said shareholders heard “plenty” from him in September, when he stepped down as Berkshire’s chairman and handed the role to Howard. So he kept…
items.t: Warren Buffett is giving $5.4 billion to his family foundations for Thanksgiving. His advice to everyone else: ‘Be a benefactor for someone else’

items.title: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars. 

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune .

Blue Cloud Ventures led the round, bringing Numa’s total funding to $96 million. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participated. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson. The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare,…
items.t: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind

items.title: McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity
items.summary:
On Nov. 6, the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency announced up to $2 billion to buy strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile. DLA aims to create targeted demand signals to enable domestic production. In fact, the United States produces a small fraction of many of the critical minerals it uses, including less than 1% of the most common type of rare-earth magnet it uses. In other words, these products are among America’s “Achilles’ Heels.”

The global market for solving these vulnerabilities is huge. More than $4 trillion of global imports, nearly a quarter of the total, sit in what our new research calls the Achilles’ heel of global trade: products that face at least two of three vulnerabilities. They are critical to economic activity, they come from a handful of suppliers, or they come from geopolitically distant partners. For business, they can also be a map of where the next growth opportunities lie.

Companies are moving, for example by finding ways to have alternative sources of rare earths outside of China and by pooling purchasing commitments for generic drugs. Software companies now sell visibility into suppliers several tiers upstream.

The next era of globalization is not about retreat; it is about reconfiguration. In 2025, U.S.–China goods trade fell nearly 30%, yet total U.S. imports and Chinese exports reached new highs, and trade is now traveling shorter geopolitical distances as economies shift toward more closely aligned partners. So businesses need to understand where that reconfiguration is most likely to happen, and much of it could…
items.t: McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity

items.title: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?
items.summary:
Good morning, it’s Finance Editor Jeff Roberts in for Allie. In the course of my career, I’ve interviewed hundreds of venture capitalists, and I have an observation: Many VCs regard themselves as unconventional thinkers, but when it comes to the norms of their industry, they are highly conformist. Bradley Tusk is not one of those VCs.

Brash and outspoken, Tusk made his name as the chief of staff for former New York City mayor Mike Bloomberg, and by helping Uber in its early battles with city officials and the taxi industry. Soon after, he leveraged his reputation as a political fixer to launch Tusk Ventures, which helped startups like Lemonade, Bird, FanDuel, Ro, and Coinbase navigate various regulatory minefields.

In 2025, Tusk made another bold bet. Despite a successful run as a conventional VC, which saw Tusk raise $300 million over three funds, he decided to abandon the model in favor of something novel: taking equity in exchange for services rather than cash. 

“I took half a step back and asked, ‘What do I and don’t I like about this process?’ I like two things: I like legalizing disruptive shit, and I like betting on and working with founders who are interesting. What I did not like was raising money, dealing with LPs, taking board seats, and portfolio construction. I also didn’t like giving someone else 80% of my profits,” Tusk explains.

In practice, Tusk says the pivot means his firm spends almost all of its time on a few core areas. Those include helping startups obtain licenses and navigate regulations, and turning up on fundraising calls to assure would-be…
items.t: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?

Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes

items.title: Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit
items.summary:
From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair?

For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

Continue reading...
items.t: Christmas ‘dupes’: the cheaper gift versions proving a festive hit in the cost of living crisis

items.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
items.summary:
Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn, announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social…
items.t: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris

items.title: Troubled Scottish steel supplier raises questions over Royal Navy contracts
items.summary:
Liberty Steel Dalzell plant in Motherwell with order for 34,000 tonnes of metal plate to build three warships has struggled to pay bills

The Royal Navy is facing questions over whether three new warships will be built with British steel as its Scottish supplier faces deepening financial difficulties.

Liberty Steel Dalzell, a plate mill in Motherwell, has struggled to pay its bills and workers in recent weeks, according to several people with knowledge of operations.

items.title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business
items.summary:
Exclusive: British sportswear firm is seeking to obtain rights to The Conditioning Club, which is also the name of a Gloucestershire gym

Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.

Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.

items.title: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab
items.summary:
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.
